prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an interesting and timely problem: how to adapt concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation-model features when the deployment distribution shifts and only unlabeled target data are available. The paper’s central claim is that concept bottlenecks are not inherently robust under shift, and that one can recover both accuracy and concept alignment through a source-free test-time adaptation procedure that updates concept vectors, the concept-to-label predictor, and a residual concept branch. Overall, I found the problem well motivated, the empirical phenomenon plausible and important, and the proposed method reasonably novel at the intersection of CBMs, foundation models, and test-time adaptation. At the same time, I have substantial concerns about the conceptual framing, the rigor of the theoretical section, and several aspects of the empirical validation and interpretation claims. My overall assessment is positive but cautious.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation at a high level. The paper identifies a real gap in the literature: recent CBM work often emphasizes interpretability and sometimes source-domain accuracy, while robustness under deployment shift is much less studied, especially in the foundation-model regime. The observation that CBMs can underperform direct feature-based predictors under shift, despite matching them in-domain, is important and worth documenting. The proposed decomposition into three adaptation components is also intuitively appealing: concept-score alignment for low-level perturbations, label-layer adaptation for changed concept-label relations, and residual concepts for incompleteness of the original concept bank. This decomposition gives the method a clear narrative and makes the ablation section easier to interpret.

The empirical results are also promising on their face. Across several datasets and multiple CBM construction methods, CONDA often improves target-domain AVG and WG substantially, especially on Waterbirds and Metashift where the unadapted CBMs degrade sharply. The fact that the method is evaluated with different concept-bank construction pipelines is a strength, because it suggests the approach is not tied to one specific CBM instantiation. The use of worst-group accuracy is also appropriate for spurious-correlation benchmarks. The interpretability discussion, especially the emergence of bird-related residual concepts on Waterbirds, is suggestive and potentially valuable.

That said, the paper currently overstates both its formalism and some of its empirical conclusions. My main concern is that the theoretical framing in Section 2 is not yet sufficiently precise or useful to support the later algorithmic choices. The definitions of “low-level shift” and “concept-level shift” are effectively defined in terms of whether the chosen concept mapping preserves or changes the concept-score distribution and whether the prediction distribution changes. This makes the taxonomy somewhat circular and model-relative rather than a property of the data-generating process. In particular, “low-level shift” is defined as one that does not change the concept-score distribution under a given concept mapping, but then the failure mode of a “non-robust concept bottleneck under low-level shift” is exactly that the concept-score distribution does change. This is not a contradiction if interpreted carefully, but it makes the terminology confusing: the shift type is being defined by what an ideal concept mapping should do, while the failure mode is defined by what the actual mapping does. As written, the formalism does not cleanly separate properties of the environment from properties of the model.

Relatedly, Definition 1 on completeness is too weak and too broad to be operational. It says a concept set is complete if there exists a classifier mapping concepts to labels that equalizes prediction distributions across source and target under low-level and concept-level shifts. But equality of prediction distributions is not the same as correctness, and the definition depends on the target domain in a way that makes “completeness” deployment-specific rather than intrinsic to the concept set. Also, because the classifier class is broad and the prediction distribution is unconditional, this notion may be satisfied in degenerate ways. I do not think this definition currently provides a meaningful theoretical foundation for the residual concept branch. The paper would be stronger if it either substantially sharpened these definitions or presented them more modestly as intuition rather than formal characterization.

A second major concern is the reliance on pseudo-labels from non-interpretable predictors, especially an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe FM predictions, while claiming adaptation of the interpretable CBM “without sacrificing utility” and aligning with non-interpretable classification. In practice, the method appears to inherit robustness from the FM-based pseudo-labeler. This is not inherently a flaw, but it changes the interpretation of the contribution. The method is less a purely concept-centric adaptation mechanism and more a distillation/adaptation procedure that transfers target-domain signal from stronger black-box predictors into the CBM. The paper acknowledges this partially, but not enough. A key question is: how much of the gain comes from the adaptation machinery versus simply trusting the FM pseudo-labeler directly? Since the pseudo-labels are chosen from the more confident of zero-shot and linear-probe predictions, the method may be benefiting from a strong oracle-like teacher. The comparisons in Table 1 show that CONDA often approaches LP/ZS performance, but the paper should more directly quantify the dependence on pseudo-label quality and compare against simpler baselines such as training only the CBM label layer on those pseudo-labels, or directly using the pseudo-label ensemble as the final predictor.

This issue is especially important because the source-free setting is described as not having access to source data, yet the method assumes access to source-trained linear probes and source-domain class-conditional Gaussian statistics in concept space. These are reasonable artifacts to store, but they should be counted as source-side information. The paper should be explicit that the method is source-data-free, not source-information-free. In addition, the CSA step assumes class-conditional Gaussianity of concept scores and availability of invertible covariance estimates. For high-dimensional concept spaces or classes with limited source samples, covariance estimation can be unstable. The paper does not discuss whether diagonal covariance, shrinkage, or regularization is used, nor how sensitive results are to these choices. This matters because the Mahalanobis objective is central to the method’s first stage.

There are also some methodological ambiguities and possible inconsistencies. Equation (5) defines the target CBM correctly, but later text refers to Eqn. (3) when discussing the target-domain CBM in Section 3.2, which appears to be a numbering error. The Mahalanobis distance formula in Section 3.1 seems to have a parenthesis typo. These are minor, but they contribute to a sense that the technical presentation needs tightening. More importantly, the online adaptation protocol can be vulnerable to order effects and error accumulation, especially with pseudo-labels. The paper follows standard TTA practice, but it should report sensitivity to batch order, batch size, and episodic versus online adaptation more prominently in the main paper, not only in appendices. Since the method updates concept vectors and residual concepts online, drift could be substantial.

On the empirical side, the results are encouraging but not fully convincing yet. First, the paper compares CONDA-enhanced CBMs mainly against unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable ZS/LP baselines. What is missing are stronger TTA baselines adapted to the same setting. For example, one would like to see comparisons to applying standard TTA methods directly to the CBM label layer, to the concept vectors, or to the combined linear map WC over frozen FM features. Since the final CBM predictor is still linear in FM features, a natural baseline is source-free adaptation of a linear classifier on top of frozen FM embeddings using the same pseudo-labels and online protocol. Without such baselines, it is hard to know whether the concept-specific design is necessary for the observed gains. The paper cites CAFA and other TTA methods as inspiration, but does not appear to benchmark against them in a matched setup.

Second, some results complicate the narrative. On CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 with the Yeh et al. CBM, CONDA sometimes hurts target performance relative to the unadapted CBM. On Waterbirds, CONDA applied to the CBM of Yuksekgonul et al. improves dramatically over the unadapted CBM but still does not surpass the zero-shot baseline. On Metashift, CONDA nearly closes the gap to ZS, which is impressive, but this may partly reflect the strength of the pseudo-label teacher. These mixed outcomes are acceptable, but the paper should analyze failure cases more deeply rather than emphasizing only the positive trend. In particular, when does CSA hurt? When does RCB overfit? When does pseudo-label noise dominate?

Third, the interpretability claims need more rigorous support. The paper argues that adapted concepts are “better aligned with the test data” and that residual concepts improve interpretability. However, the evidence presented in the main text is largely anecdotal and qualitative. If interpretability is a central claim, the paper should include quantitative measures: concept coherency, redundancy, sparsity, stability across runs, human evaluation of concept labels, or intervention-based faithfulness tests. The fact that land-related concepts become positively associated with “waterbird” after adaptation may reflect adaptation to target correlations, but whether this is desirable depends on the benchmark and the intended semantics of the concepts. If the target domain itself contains shifted spurious correlations, adapting explanations to match them is not obviously an interpretability improvement. More generally, there is tension between adapting to target correlations for accuracy and preserving semantically meaningful, causally relevant concepts. The paper should discuss this tension more explicitly.

I also have concerns about the residual concept branch from an interpretability standpoint. Once residual concepts are randomly initialized and optimized only through pseudo-labeled target loss plus similarity/coherency regularization, they may become useful latent directions rather than human-meaningful concepts. The paper’s automated annotation procedure may assign plausible names post hoc, but this does not guarantee semantic validity. Since the residual branch is effectively adding capacity to the model, one must ask whether it remains a concept bottleneck in a meaningful sense or becomes a lightly constrained linear adapter. This does not invalidate the method, but it weakens the interpretability claim unless supported by stronger evidence.

A further conceptual issue is that the paper frames CSA as aligning target concept-score distributions to source class-conditional Gaussians, which is motivated as preserving the input distribution seen by the source label predictor. But if the target domain truly exhibits concept-level shift, forcing alignment to source concept statistics may be counterproductive or even semantically wrong. The ablations suggest CSA helps mainly on low-level shifts and less on concept-level shifts, which is consistent with this concern. This is not a flaw in itself, but it suggests the three-stage pipeline may benefit from an adaptive gating mechanism that first diagnoses the shift type or confidence in pseudo-labels before deciding which components to activate. As it stands, the method seems somewhat heuristic in applying all three stages sequentially regardless of scenario.

The paper would also benefit from clearer discussion of computational cost and deployment practicality in the main text. Since the method performs multiple gradient steps per batch across three stages and maintains residual concepts, the runtime and memory overhead may be nontrivial, especially for large-scale or latency-sensitive deployments. The appendix may contain complexity analysis, but some summary should appear in the main paper because test-time adaptation methods are often judged partly on practicality.

In terms of novelty, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution by bringing together CBMs and source-free TTA in the FM setting, and by proposing concept-specific adaptation components. I do not believe the individual ingredients are fundamentally new: pseudo-labeling, class-aware alignment, sparse linear adaptation, and residual concept expansion all have precedents. But the combination is sensible and the application domain is novel enough to be of interest. The main question for acceptance is therefore whether the paper demonstrates that concept-aware adaptation offers something beyond generic adaptation of a linear head on FM features. Right now, the evidence is suggestive but not definitive.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following. First, simplify and sharpen the formal section. Either provide a more standard shift taxonomy and state the failure modes informally, or make the definitions genuinely precise and non-circular. Second, add stronger baselines: generic source-free adaptation of a linear probe on FM features, adaptation of the combined CBM linear map without concept-specific regularization, and perhaps CAFA/TENT-style variants adapted to this frozen-feature setting. Third, quantify the role of pseudo-label quality, including an ablation using only zero-shot, only linear probe, self-labeling from the CBM, and confidence-thresholded pseudo-labels. Fourth, provide more rigorous interpretability evaluation, especially for residual concepts. Fifth, analyze negative cases and sensitivity to online adaptation order, covariance estimation, and hyperparameters in the main paper. Sixth, clarify what source-side artifacts are assumed available at deployment.

My overall recommendation is borderline positive. The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem, and the empirical gains on several shifted benchmarks are compelling enough to merit attention. However, the current version overclaims on theory and interpretability, and it does not yet fully establish that the proposed concept-specific adaptation is superior to simpler alternatives. If accepted, I would view it as a promising systems-and-empirics contribution with moderate methodological novelty, rather than a theoretically grounded advance.

In summary, I see clear merit in the paper’s motivation, setup, and empirical direction, but I would like to see stronger baselines, tighter formalism, and more rigorous interpretability evidence before being fully convinced.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. It identifies three failure modes for deployed CBMs: non-robust concept mappings under low-level shifts, mismatch of the concept-to-label predictor under concept-level shifts, and incompleteness of the concept bank. To address these, it proposes CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation pipeline using only unlabeled target data: (1) Concept Score Alignment (CSA), which adapts concept vectors by matching pseudo-labeled target concept scores to source class-conditional Gaussian statistics via a Mahalanobis-based loss; (2) Linear Probing Adaptation (LPA), which updates the concept-to-label linear layer using pseudo-label cross-entropy with elastic-net regularization; and (3) Residual Concept Bottleneck (RCB), which adds new residual concepts and a residual linear head optimized with classification, diversity, and coherence regularizers. Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial gains over unadapted CBMs, especially under concept-level shifts, and qualitative evidence that adapted concepts better reflect target-domain correlations.
strengths: Addresses an interesting and timely problem at the intersection of interpretability, foundation models, and test-time adaptation; the problem setting is practically relevant and relatively underexplored.
The decomposition into three failure modes provides a useful conceptual framework for thinking about why CBMs may fail under shift.
The method is modular and intuitive: adapting concept vectors, then the concept-to-label layer, then augmenting with residual concepts is a sensible design.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets, multiple shift types, multiple backbones, and multiple CBM construction methods, which strengthens the practical case for the approach.
Results show large improvements over unadapted CBMs on several benchmarks, especially Waterbirds and Metashift, where adaptation appears highly beneficial.
The paper includes some interpretability-oriented analysis, including changes in concept importance and residual concepts that appear semantically meaningful.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing of shift types is weakly connected to the actual adaptation objectives and does not yield guarantees; several definitions are more descriptive than rigorous or actionable.

The method relies heavily on pseudo-labels from zero-shot/linear-probe FM predictors, so the adaptation quality may largely depend on the robustness of these non-interpretable predictors; this weakens the claim that the CBM itself is being adapted in a principled source-free way.

The source-free setting is not fully source-free in practice because CSA assumes access to class-conditional source statistics (means/covariances) computed from labeled source data; this is a nontrivial retained artifact from the source domain.

Empirical comparisons are incomplete: there is little direct comparison against standard test-time adaptation baselines applied to the same FM+linear or FM+CBM pipelines, making it hard to isolate the novelty versus generic pseudo-label fine-tuning.

Some reported results show adaptation hurting strong CBM baselines (e.g., Yeh et al. on CIFAR10/CIFAR100/Camelyon17), suggesting instability or mismatch between components, but this is not deeply analyzed.
Interpretability claims are mostly qualitative and anecdotal; there is no rigorous quantitative metric showing that adapted or residual concepts are more faithful, stable, or human-aligned.

The online adaptation protocol may be sensitive to batch order and target stream composition, but robustness to ordering, batch size, and pseudo-label noise is not clearly established in the main paper.
methodological_flaws: The definition of low-level shift in Eq. (2) assumes the concept-score distribution is unchanged across domains. This is not a property of the data transformation alone but of the specific feature extractor and concept mapping. Using this as the defining criterion makes the taxonomy somewhat circular: if concept scores change, the shift is no longer 'low-level' by definition, which weakens the scientific logic of the failure-mode analysis.

Definition 1 of concept completeness is problematic: it defines completeness via existence of a classifier g such that source and target prediction distributions are identical. Matching prediction distributions is not equivalent to correct label prediction or sufficiency of concepts; identical marginal prediction distributions can occur even with poor accuracy. Thus the notion of completeness is not mathematically aligned with the intended semantic claim.

The CSA objective assumes class-conditional Gaussianity of source concept scores and uses stored source means/covariances, but there is no empirical validation that these distributions are approximately Gaussian or well-conditioned. In high-dimensional concept spaces, covariance estimation and inversion can be unstable, especially for classes with limited samples.

The Mahalanobis distance formula in the text appears malformed typographically, and more importantly the optimization objective log(D_intra/D_inter) is heuristic rather than derived from a principled likelihood-ratio or domain adaptation objective. No justification is given for why minimizing this ratio should align target concept distributions to source ones under pseudo-label noise.

The pseudo-labeling strategy selects the more confident prediction between zero-shot and linear probing, but confidence across different models is generally not calibrated or directly comparable. This can introduce systematic pseudo-label bias without analysis or calibration.

The residual branch is claimed to improve interpretability, but residual concepts are randomly initialized and optimized only through classification plus similarity/coherence regularizers on unlabeled target data. There is no guarantee these vectors correspond to semantically meaningful concepts rather than arbitrary discriminative directions.

The coherence regularizer in Eq. (13) effectively rewards high similarity to top-k target features, which may encourage prototype-like directions but does not establish concept coherence in a human-interpretable sense. The interpretability argument is therefore empirically under-supported.

The empirical section lacks stronger causal ablations to show each component addresses its claimed failure mode beyond correlation. For example, CSA alone sometimes outperforms the full method, and adaptation sometimes degrades performance, indicating interactions that are not theoretically or empirically resolved.

The comparison to non-interpretable baselines is not fully fair for the central claim of 'aligning CBM performance with non-interpretable classification' because the pseudo-labels themselves are derived from those non-interpretable predictors, effectively importing their decision boundary into the CBM.

No statistical significance testing is provided beyond mean ± std, and it is unclear over what randomness the variance is computed. Given some gains are modest and some degradations occur, stronger empirical validity checks would be desirable.
